interest: Tracks 1937-39 corporate lobbying over Japan's exchange controls, blocked yen, and the North China yen-bloc currency scheme.
overview: This file consists of the official Department of State 'List of Papers' (docket sheets 6 through 26, sub-numbers 40 to 189) for Decimal File 894.5151, covering the period from September 1937 to December 1939. The register indexes correspondence, telegrams, despatches, and inter-departmental memoranda documenting the implementation and impact of Japanese foreign exchange control legislation, particularly Law No. 87 of September 1937 and subsequent Finance Ministry ordinances enacted during the Second Sino-Japanese War. Primary subjects recorded include the blocking and delayed remittance into U.S. dollars of American commercial funds, revenues, and dividends held in Japan—notably affecting cotton merchants (R.L. Dixon & Brother, American Cotton Cooperative Association, Orvis Brothers & Co.), the American President Lines, and the Ford Motor Company of Japan. The docket also tracks State and Treasury Department intelligence on Japan's diminishing foreign exchange and gold reserves, Japanese efforts to peg the yen to sterling and later the U.S. dollar, and the aggressive extension of Japanese exchange and export restrictions into occupied North China (Tsingtao, Peiping, Chefoo) via the puppet Federal Reserve Bank currency and the Yokohama Specie Bank to monopolize trade and displace foreign enterprises.

subfiles.about: Official Department of State docket sheet register (List of Papers) for decimal file 894.5151, indexing incoming and outgoing documents concerning Japanese foreign exchange control and blocked American funds from September 1937 to December 1939.
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.summary: This multi-page register forms the continuous official docket list (Sheets 6 through 26) of documents filed under State Department decimal file 894.5151 from late 1937 through 1939. It records the receipt, dispatch, and purports of telegrams, diplomatic despatches, cross-reference sheets, and memoranda concerning Japan's Emergency Foreign Exchange Control Law and its impact on international trade. The entries document the severe restrictions placed on remitting foreign exchange in U.S. dollars, the blocking of profits and revenues belonging to American cotton brokers, shipping lines, and manufacturing companies, and the diplomatic representations made by the American Embassy in Tokyo. In addition, the sheets index intelligence reports on Japan's foreign exchange and gold reserves, the shift of the yen peg from sterling to the dollar, and the establishment of Japanese-controlled currency regimes in occupied China.
